dims.name: NEON LATTICE
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: top-down 2D, the whole arena on screen. An ULTRA-POLISHED twin-stick sniper duel in a dark glass arena drawn in clean neon vector light (additive glows, soft bloom halos, a reflective floor grid that pulses to the music, light that spills from every shot). renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. HOOK: line of sight is everything. Pillars and walls cast real shadow volumes: you only see the enemy while there is a clear line between you (draw the unseen area as darkness with a soft edge; a last-seen ghost marks where they vanished). Rail rounds are near-instant and RICOCHET exactly once off walls. Holding alt (FOCUS) slows you to a crawl but projects your laser sight, bounce included, across the arena — a perfect aim, and a beam the enemy can see coming. Abilities, for example: BLINK (short teleport through thin cover, leaves an afterimage) and DECOY (a hologram of you that walks on and paints a fake laser — the home dimension's decoy, reborn). Sudden death: the arena walls close in and the shadows lift.

dims.name: IRON AUTUMN
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: third person 3D, over the shoulder. SETTING: a bombed-out European town square at dusk in the autumn of 1944 — a ruined church with a bell tower, rubble-choked streets, a burnt-out tank and half-track, sandbag nests, a collapsed cafe, a dry fountain, tank traps; about 120 m end to end with trenches, craters and broken walls giving covered lanes for anyone who wants to work closer. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. It should look like a war film: low sun through smoke with light shafts, drifting ash and embers, searchlights sweeping the cloud base, flak bursts and a formation of bombers crossing overhead, a desaturated grade with warm highlights, bloom, grain and vignette. Period bolt-action scoped rifles; the snipers wear long coats and helmets with a scarf / armband in their identity colour. No real-world insignia, flags, symbols or named units anywhere. THE WORLD INTERFERES: an artillery barrage walks across the square at intervals (positions and timing a pure function of the seed and ctx.time; each shell telegraphed by a rising whistle and a ground marker, lethal only at the centre) so nobody can camp one spot forever; the church bell tolls; a wall collapses late in the round. alt = SCOPE: a period reticle with breathing sway — and a lens glint the other sniper can see. Bullets are fast but not instant and drop slightly. Abilities, for example: SMOKE grenade and HELMET-ON-A-STICK (raise a decoy helmet from cover; if it draws a shot, the shooter's muzzle flash is marked for you) or a parachute FLARE that lights up and marks an area. Kill moment: slow motion, the helmet rings and spins away, dust falls from the rafters, the bell tolls once.

dims.name: INK CITY
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: third person 3D, over-the-shoulder, rendered as a living COMIC BOOK. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. Two snipers on opposing clusters of city rooftops (water towers, billboards, AC units, skylights, a street canyon between them, 60-100 m apart) at a lurid sunset. The look is the point: flat cel shading with two or three tone steps, thick ink outlines (inverted hull or a post-process edge pass), Ben-Day halftone dots in the shadows and sky, a paper-grain overlay and a panel border; onomatopoeia that pops into the world as drawn lettering when things happen (BLAM! KRAK! WHIFF! THUD!), speed lines when you aim, a caption box for the reload. alt = AIM: the camera punches in over the shoulder into an inset comic panel with the scope view (or a hard zoom with radial speed lines). Abilities, for example: LEAP (a rocket-boot or grapple jump to another roof, drawn with a motion arc) and SMOKE BOMB (a hand-drawn POOF! cloud that blocks sight — the home dimension's smoke). Kill moment: a freeze-frame splash panel — halftone burst, the victim knocked out of frame in a spray of ink stars, giant lettering.

dims.name: CARTRIDGE CANYON
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: side-on 2D, SUPER RETRO pixel art, a small single-screen arena with both snipers always visible. renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. Render the game to a small off-screen framebuffer (about 320x180, kept at 16:9 with themed letterbox bars on other aspect ratios) and blit it up with nearest-neighbour scaling; a strict 16-colour-ish palette; chunky animated sprites drawn in code (idle, run, jump, crouch, prone, recoil); a tile-built canyon with two cliffs, ledges, crates and a rope bridge; parallax mountains and clouds; a hand-made bitmap font; optional scanlines and a subtle CRT curve on the upscale. Bullets are visible pixels that travel fast with a little DROP over distance, so long shots need holdover. alt = PRONE/STEADY (smaller target, steadier aim, cannot move). Abilities, for example: JETPACK hop and a SMOKE grenade or throwable DECOY cardboard cut-out. Chiptune music (square lead, triangle bass, noise drums) and crunchy 8-bit sfx. Kill moment: the classic — the victim flashes, pops into pixel confetti, and a big dithered banner slams in.

dims.name: BREAK POINT
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: third person 3D chase camera. SETTING: gloriously absurd — two snipers duel while riding SURFBOARDS on a huge rolling ocean swell off a tropical beach at golden hour. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. The ocean is the star and must be beautiful: a Gerstner-wave surface (its height a pure function of position and ctx.time, so both clients ride the same sea) with foam on the crests, light glowing through the wave faces, spray, sun glitter and a sky to match; a palm-lined beach, a pier, a lifeguard tower and a lighthouse on rocks frame the bay. THE WAVES MOVE YOU, and that is the heart of how this world plays: you carve left and right across the swell, gain speed dropping down a face and lose it climbing, and can run down the line to close the distance or pull away; every swell lifts, carries and tilts the board, a breaking crest shoves you along with it, whitewater slows and wobbles you, and reading the sea to pick your line is as much of the skill as the shot. This is strictly a THIRD-PERSON world (the surfer and the board are always on screen): the world that follows it is first person, and the two must feel nothing alike. HOOK: the sea is the cover. Wave crests rise BETWEEN the two snipers and hide them from each other; you shoot in the windows when both of you are up on a crest or the trough opens, and your aim bobs and rolls with the board. Rounds skip off the water in a line of splashes. alt = BRACE: drop to one knee — steadier aim, but you cannot carve. THE WORLD INTERFERES and delights: dolphins leaping through the line of fire, a flock of gulls, a beach ball on the wind, a banner plane, a circling shark fin, a cruise ship sounding its horn, and every so often a monster set wave that both of you have to deal with (all timed from the seed and ctx.time). Abilities, for example: DUCK DIVE (plunge under the surface for a second — untargetable — and pop up further along) and SPRAY WALL (a hard cutback that throws a curtain of spray that blocks sight: the smoke grenade of the sea) or CHUM the gulls onto the enemy to mark them. KILL MOMENT, which is also a hand-off (this world is always followed by the underwater world THE DEEP, through a transition called 'plunge' that starts from your last frame): play it as one natural, continuous beat across the whole 'over' phase. The hit surfer loses the board — it fires into the sky — and they fall, properly: arms out, tumbling down the wave face into the sea with a towering splash, a rainbow in the mist. The winner sees them go under, steps off their own board and DIVES in after them, a clean header. The camera follows the winner down the face and through the surface, so that the LAST FRAME of the round is the lens crossing the waterline: foam and bubbles filling the frame, the bright surface just overhead, blue below. Both players see the same shot. Nothing may pop or cut; it must read as 'he fell in, and I went in after him'.

dims.name: THE DEEP
dims.brief: THIS IS THE BEST-LOOKING WORLD IN THE GAME: the owner asked for it by name and wants it to be the showpiece, so spend your effort on the picture and on the feeling of being under water before anything else, and then tune it until it holds frame rate. PERSPECTIVE: first person, fully 3D, underwater — and above all IMMERSIVE: the player should feel submerged. SETTING: two rival SPEARFISHERS with band-powered spearguns hunt each other over a reef wall that drops away into the deep: sunlit shallows and a kelp forest above, a sunken fishing boat on a ledge, coral heads and rock arches for cover, and below everything a blue-black abyss. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. THE OCEAN MUST FEEL ALIVE: shafts of sunlight slanting down through the surface and moving with the swell; animated caustics over sand, coral and hull; drifting marine snow; swaying kelp; depth fog in blue-green that swallows everything past about 70 m; a visible rippling surface overhead. FISH EVERYWHERE: several schools that flow as shoals, part around the divers and scatter at a shot; reef fish among the coral; a turtle, a manta gliding past, a curious shark that circles but never bites. DEEP-SEA CREATURES BELOW: looking down into the abyss you see glowing shapes — anglerfish lures, jellyfish pulsing with bioluminescence, a huge slow silhouette. AND THE KRAKEN (required, the set-piece of this world): at least one truly GIANT kraken — body the size of the wreck, long tentacles, a great pale eye — that swims a slow patrol beneath and sometimes above both players, on a path timed from the seed and ctx.time so both clients see the same thing. Its shadow passes over the reef and dims the light; its tentacles rise through the arena and act as huge moving cover that blocks sightlines and spears; when it passes close it rolls its eye toward the nearer diver; a spear that hits it makes it jet a blinding ink cloud; a tentacle that touches a diver shoves them hard and knocks their aim, but it NEVER kills — only a spear from the other sniper scores. Give it weight: slow, enormous, rumbling sub-bass, a wake that shakes the kelp and scatters the fish. MOVEMENT is true 3D swimming with glide and weight: you swim where you look, JUMP kicks you upward, and you sink slowly when still. HOOK: bubbles and patience. Spears are slow, visible bolts with drag that sink a little and trail bubbles pointing straight back at whoever fired; one spear loaded at a time with a real reload. You exhale a puff of bubbles every few seconds that rises and gives your position away; holding alt (HOLD BREATH) raises the sight, zooms and stops your bubbles until your air gauge says otherwise. The wreck's holds, the arches and the kelp give covered routes for closing the distance; the open water over the drop-off is where the long shots happen. Abilities, for example: SONAR PING (a pulse that outlines the other diver through the murk for two seconds and tells them they were pinged: the recon tool) and SILT CLOUD (kick up a blinding cloud: smoke) or a drifting GLOW-STICK decoy. Sound matters here: muffled, breathing, the click of the speargun, whale song far off, the kraken's rumble. Kill moment: slow motion, the spear's bubble trail hanging in the water, the victim's mask and fins drifting away as they tumble upward in a column of bubbles through a shaft of light, the fish scattering — and the kraken's eye turning to watch. ARRIVAL (the 'intro' phase): this world normally follows the surfing world, where the loser has just fallen off a board into the sea and the winner dived in after them; a transition called 'plunge' ends on your first frame. So open just below the surface, looking down the reef wall, with the surface boiling with fresh bubbles overhead, and let both divers sink into their starting places through the light shafts during the intro, pulling their masks down and loading the first spear, with the kraken's shape already moving far below. It must also make sense when the world is reached from somewhere else.

dims.name: COIN-OP DEADEYE
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: first person, as a late-1990s ARCADE-CABINET sniper game (an affectionate, entirely original take on the light-gun-sniper genre — not a copy of any real cabinet: invent the title, logo, city and characters). renderer 'three', aim 'look'. THE LOOK: chunky low-poly downtown with flat and Gouraud shading, tiny textures, a little vertex snapping and wobble, a low internal resolution scaled up crisp, ordered dithering, a saturated arcade palette; and a LOUD arcade HUD drawn by you: PLAYER 1 / PLAYER 2 in the snipers' colours, a giant round timer, a blinking INSERT COIN, score pop-ups that slam in ('LONG SHOT +3000', 'NICE!', 'TOO SLOW'), stage banners, a credit counter. THE SIGNATURE: a big circular SCOPE LENS floats over the middle of the screen showing a magnified view while the rest of the screen shows the wide shot around it — you sweep the lens across the city to find the other sniper, and alt pushes the magnification higher (narrower, shakier). Each sniper works a string of perches along their side of an avenue — rooftops, a billboard gantry, a window-cleaning cradle, a crane cab — and can ZIP to the next one to close the gap or fall back; cut-out civilians and pigeons pop up in windows and on roofs like a shooting gallery (shoot one and you eat a reload penalty and a 'DON'T SHOOT CIVILIANS!' banner). A blimp carries the live score, traffic crawls below, fireworks or a news helicopter cross the sightline. Abilities, for example: ZIPLINE (move perch) and POP-UP DECOY (a cut-out of you springs up on another perch). Arcade sound: big sampled-feeling hits, an excitable chiptune-meets-rock loop. Kill moment: 'PERFECT!' stamps across the screen, the lens freezes on the hit, a score tally rattles up and coins shower.

dims.name: RUBBER HOSE RIDGE
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: side-on 2D platformer. SETTING: a 1930s rubber-hose cartoon come to life (the era's general style — noodle limbs, big gloves, everything bouncing to the beat — with ORIGINAL characters of your own invention; do not imitate any studio's actual characters or trademarks). renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. Black, white and warm grey like an old print, with each sniper's identity colour as the only tint; ink outlines that boil slightly every few frames; film grain, gate weave, scratches, a soft vignette. EVERYTHING dances: the cacti, the sun, the mesas and both snipers bob in time with a ragtime / hot-jazz piano loop. The stage is a desert canyon full of slapstick machinery: springboards, a seesaw rock, a painted tunnel on a cliff face, a wobbling tower of crates, a handcar on a rail, ladders and ledges on two mesas with a long open gap between. Rifles are cork pop-guns: the cork is a visible projectile that arcs, so range takes judgement; one bonk wins. alt = TAKE AIM: the barrel telescopes out comically — the longer you hold, the flatter and faster the shot, but you are rooted to the spot. SLAPSTICK INTERFERES (timed from the seed and ctx.time, always telegraphed): an anvil whistles down onto a shadow, a train bursts out of the painted tunnel, a tumbleweed bowls through, a vulture steals a hat. Abilities, for example: PORTABLE HOLE (slap a black disc on the ground, drop in, pop out of its twin somewhere else) and DECOY SIGN (plant a wooden cut-out of yourself that waves) or a spring-loaded BOXING GLOVE that swats a cork out of the air. Kill moment: the victim is left scorched and blinking with stars and birds circling, their hat lands last, and an iris begins to close on them.

dims.name: INK DUEL
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: the side-on 'belt-scroll brawler' plane — the camera looks along a wide street from the side and you move left and right AND in and out of depth, the way a classic beat-'em-up plays — framed as a living page of Japanese MANGA (the art form, with original characters and setting). renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. Pure black ink on warm paper: bold brush outlines with varying weight, screentone dot shading in several densities, hatching, speed lines, white gouache highlights; each sniper carries a single spot of their identity colour and nothing else is coloured. The play field sits inside inked panel borders, and CUT-IN PANELS slide over the page for the big beats: an extreme close-up of narrowed eyes when you focus, a hand working the bolt, a tall panel for the muzzle flash — with sound effects lettered in big brush katakana (for example ドン! バン! ザッ ゴゴゴ) as part of the artwork. SETTING: a long rain-lashed back street and shrine bridge at night, about three screens wide (the camera frames both snipers and zooms as they separate): lanterns, vending machines, parked scooters, stacked crates, a torii gate, cats on walls, rain drawn as ink strokes, and a train that thunders across an overpass at intervals (timed from the seed and ctx.time), blocking the long sightline and drowning out sound. The duel: shots travel across the plane to the point you aim at, depth included; cover is whatever sits in your lane; you can hold the far end and thread a long shot, or sprint and weave lane to lane to get close. alt = FOCUS: concentration lines close in, the aim line steadies and extends, you slow to a walk. Abilities, for example: FLASH STEP (a short blink that leaves an afterimage and speed lines) and SUBSTITUTION (vanish in a puff, leaving a decoy that takes the shot: the decoy and the smoke in one). Kill moment: a full-bleed splash page — both figures frozen in silhouette, a black impact burst with white speed lines, one enormous sound effect, an umbrella tumbling away.

dims.name: LITTLE PLANETS
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: 2D side-on in deep space, the whole system on screen. renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. Each sniper stands on the surface of a tiny planetoid and walks around its circumference (left / right = clockwise / anticlockwise); a handful of planetoids, moons and one heavy gas giant hang between them, slowly orbiting (positions are a pure function of ctx.time). HOOK: bullets are slow enough to see and are bent by every body's GRAVITY — you snipe AROUND planets with curving shots. A dotted trajectory preview shows the start of the arc; holding alt (STEADY) extends the preview at the cost of standing still. Abilities, for example: JETPACK (leap off your rock and coast to another planetoid, landing feet-first) and PROBE (launch a little satellite that orbits and lights the enemy up — the recon tool) or a one-shot SHIELD bubble. The bot must aim with physics: sample candidate angles, simulate each trajectory, pick the best, then add skill-scaled error. Art direction: cosy, stylized space — flat-shaded planets with rings and craters, parallax starfield, soft nebula gradients, glowing comet-trail bullets, tiny astronaut snipers. Sudden death: a black hole opens at the centre and grows, dragging shots and rocks inward.

dims.name: NIGHT WINDOWS
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: first person, through the scope, in a rain-soaked monochrome FILM NOIR city with one accent colour per sniper. renderer '2d' (drawn in layers; no three.js needed) or 'three' — your call; aim 'look'. Two apartment blocks face each other across a street. Each sniper hides somewhere in a grid of dark windows (about 6 x 4) of their own building and sees the opposite facade. You pan your view across the far building looking for a shape that should not be there. HOOK: information warfare. Moving to an adjacent window takes about a second and can be seen as a passing silhouette; holding alt raises the SCOPE (you must be scoped to make the shot at this range) but your lens GLINTS when it points near the enemy; lightning (timed from ctx.time and the seed, so both clients agree) floods every window with light for an instant. Abilities, for example: LAMP (switch on a light with a mannequin silhouette in another of your windows — a decoy that draws fire) and BLACKOUT (kill the street lights for a few seconds) or a camera FLASH that blinds a scoped enemy. One shot, one window. Look: high-contrast black and white, venetian-blind shadows, rain streaks, neon sign reflections in wet brick, film grain, a letterboxed frame, a lonely saxophone-ish lead over brushed drums. Kill moment: the window shatters in slow motion, the silhouette drops, the neon sign flickers.

dims.name: TTY DUEL
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: top-down, but the ENTIRE game is rendered as TEXT — a monospace character grid on a glowing phosphor CRT (green or amber by seed, with the two snipers' identity colours standing out), with bloom, scanlines, flicker, slight barrel distortion and a blinking cursor. renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. The map is a roguelike-style facility of long corridors, pillars and rooms built from box-drawing characters; fog of war by line of sight (unseen cells dim, remembered walls stay as faint glyphs). Each sniper is an '@'; movement is smooth-stepped on the grid; the rifle fires along any angle and the shot is drawn as a ray of line characters that lingers and fades, with '*' sparks where it hits. A side log types out events in terminal voice ('> shot fired', '> miss (wall)', '> you hear footsteps: east'). alt = HOLD BREATH: a longer aim line drawn in characters. Abilities as commands, for example: `ping` (a sonar sweep that reveals the enemy as a blip for two seconds and reveals YOU to them — the home dimension's UAV) and `fork` (spawn a decoy '@' that walks off) or `rm wall` (delete a wall segment). Kill moment: the victim's '@' becomes 'x', the screen tears, and 'SEGMENTATION FAULT (core dumped)' types itself across the screen.

dims.name: TOY BOX
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: isometric 3D diorama (orthographic camera, fixed three-quarter view, whole battlefield on screen). renderer 'three', aim 'pointer'. Two plastic toy soldiers — one amber, one teal, moulded bases and all — duel across a child's bedroom floor at dusk: wooden alphabet blocks, a stack of books, dominoes, crayons, a toy train on a loop of track (moving cover, position a pure function of ctx.time), a desk lamp throwing a warm pool of light with soft shadows. Sell the miniature scale: tilt-shift blur at the top and bottom of the frame, shallow-depth-of-field feel, glossy plastic highlights, huge soft props, dust motes in the lamp light. Aiming: on desktop project the mouse onto the floor plane; with a stick, map the stick direction through the camera to a floor direction; show a thin laser dot / line. Shots are fast plastic pellets with a tiny travel time that ping off wood. alt = BRACE (kneel: steadier and longer sight line, but you cannot move). Abilities, for example: COMBAT ROLL and WIND-UP COPTER (a toy helicopter that buzzes out and spotlights the enemy for a few seconds — the home dimension's spotting drone). Kill moment: the victim bursts into plastic pieces that clatter across the floorboards while the camera does a little crane move.

dims.name: THE LONG BOLT
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: side-on 2D, flat, as a medieval EMBROIDERED TAPESTRY come to life. renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. Two crossbow sharpshooters on opposing castle towers and battlements across a valley of stitched hills, a river and a windmill; everything is drawn as needlework on linen — visible weave texture, chain-stitch outlines, a limited wool palette (madder red, woad blue, weld yellow, undyed cream), a decorative border of beasts along the top and bottom, figures in flat profile with stiff, charming two-frame animation. HOOK: ballistics you read with your eyes, like the home dimension. Bolts fly in ARCS under gravity and are pushed by a WIND that changes every round and gusts over time (a pure function of ctx.time): banners, the windmill's sails and drifting stitched clouds show its strength and direction; there is no number. alt = STEADY: a short stitched arc previews the first part of the flight. Abilities, for example: PAVISE (plant a tall shield that stops one bolt) and FALCON (a bird that flies out and circles above the enemy — the scout) or a fire-bolt that burns away a hoarding. You move along the battlements, down ladders and across a bridge. Captions in mock-Latin embroidered lettering appear for events (HIC SAGITTARIVS ERRAT). Kill moment: the victim topples in profile, a banner unfurls with a caption, and loose threads unravel from the cloth.

dims.name: PETRI DISH
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: top-down 2D under a microscope. renderer '2d', aim 'pointer'. The duel has shrunk to two single-celled snipers hunting each other in a drop of pond water, seen through a round microscope eyepiece: soft translucent blobs with wobbling membranes and drifting organelles, depth-of-field haze, chromatic fringing at the edge of the lens, caustic light ripples, dust on the glass. HOOK: camouflage in a crowd. The dish is full of harmless drifting cells that look almost exactly like the snipers; a slow current (a flow field that is a pure function of position and ctx.time) carries everything. While you drift with the current you are indistinguishable; swimming against it, or firing, makes your membrane flush with your identity colour for a moment. Shots are slow, visible protein harpoons that are pushed by the current too. alt = STILL: stop swimming and extend a faint aiming flagellum. Abilities, for example: MITOSIS (split off a decoy copy that swims away convincingly) and PULSE (a ring that makes every living sniper — you included — glow as it passes: the recon ping). The bot must play the hiding game too. Kill moment: the victim cell bursts into a bloom of bubbles and its organelles drift away while the eyepiece refocuses.

dims.name: FLAT OUT
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: first person — but the world is FLAT. A real 3D space you walk and look around in, drawn entirely as clean 2D vector illustration: flat colour fills, thick black ink outlines on every edge, no gradients, no textures, no lighting falloff, like standing inside a graphic-novel panel or a papercraft diorama. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. The owner's reference for the feel is a flat-shaded tactical shooter still (a grey concourse corridor with a slanted wall sign opening onto a sunlit container yard, an orange and a blue shipping container, a teammate drawn as a flat outlined figure, a flat outlined rifle in the corner of the view, a compass strip and a tidy minimal HUD) and paper-cut-out adventure games; take the STYLE only and invent everything else — no existing game's characters, names or layouts. Build it with unlit materials and true outlines (inverted hulls, an edge pass, or line geometry — whichever gives crisp, even-weight lines at any distance); the first-person rifle is a flat outlined drawing; snipers are flat paper cut-outs with bold outlines, a coloured band in their identity colour, and a visibly paper-thin edge when seen from the side. SETTING: a shipping-container yard between two low concourse buildings about 80 m apart — stacked containers in four or five flat colours make lanes and corners, with cranes, forklifts and gulls drawn the same way; a gantry crane carries a container across the yard on a timetable (moving cover, from ctx.time). HOOK: you are made of paper. Facing the enemy you are a full-size target; turn EDGE-ON (an ability: you rotate side-on for a second or two) and you are a thin line that is almost impossible to hit — but you cannot shoot while edge-on. Bullets punch neat round holes through thin cover (cardboard walls, signs, paper standees) that stay for the round and let both players see and shoot through them (holes are events, so both clients agree); steel containers stop everything. Every shot leaves a dashed drawn trajectory line hanging in the air for a moment, so a miss tells the other player where you are. alt = SCOPE (a flat drawn scope ring and reticle; narrower view, slower turn). Abilities, for example: EDGE-ON and STANDEE (prop up a life-size cardboard cut-out of yourself: the decoy). In-world UI in the same flat style: a compass strip, a paper ammo tag, drawn range callouts. Kill moment: the victim crumples like a ball of paper, bounces once and unfolds flat on the ground while paper scraps flutter down; the camera does a slow, flat, storybook push-in.

dims.name: WHITEOUT
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: top-down, in real 3D — a camera high above the world looking almost straight down, with perspective, so tall pines lean away from the centre of the screen with parallax and everything casts long shadows. renderer 'three', aim 'pointer' (on desktop project the mouse onto the ground; with a stick, aim along the stick). SETTING: a frozen pine forest around a small lake at dawn: low golden sun, long blue shadows across untouched snow, drifting flakes, breath clouds, a woodcutter's hut with a smoking chimney, log piles, boulders, a fallen tree across a stream, a frozen lake that creaks. The whole arena is on screen (the camera eases to keep both snipers in frame). Make the snow the star: soft shaded drifts, sparkle, depth; real shadow maps; instanced trees whose canopies sway and shed snow when a round passes through. HOOK: tracks. Every step presses a footprint into the snow and the trail stays, so your route is written on the ground for the other sniper to read; moving slowly (alt = STALK: a low crawl that also steadies your aim) leaves only faint marks, and fresh snowfall gradually fills old tracks (a pure function of ctx.time). Trunks and rocks block shots and sight; a sniper standing under a pine canopy is hidden from the camera above (the enemy sees only swaying branches and whatever tracks lead in) while you see yourself as a ghosted outline. Shots are fast tracers that kick up a line of snow and knock the snow off any branch they pass — a miss marks the tree you fired from. THE WORLD INTERFERES (timed from the seed and ctx.time): a herd of deer wanders across and scatters at gunfire, laying false trails; an owl crosses; the lake ice cracks under anyone who lingers, slowing them; and now and then a squall blows through and whites out the middle of the map for a few seconds. Abilities, for example: SNOWBALL (lob one to drop a fake set of prints and a puff where it lands: the decoy) and WHITE SHEET (lie still under a sheet and vanish from above until you move or fire: the camouflage). Kill moment: slow motion, the tracer crosses the clearing, the victim's hat flies off in a burst of powder and they flop back into a perfect snow angel as the trees shake loose their snow.

dims.name: ROTOR WASH
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: third person 3D chase camera behind your own helicopter. SETTING: two sniper helicopters duel in the sky at dawn above a sea of cloud, with mountain peaks, a radio mast and the tops of a city's towers breaking through, and weather moving across it. renderer 'three', aim 'look'. Each player flies a small two-seat helicopter and IS the sniper leaning out of its open door with a long rifle: the left stick flies (forward/back/strafe), JUMP climbs and you sink gently when you let go, the look stick aims the rifle. The sky must be beautiful: volumetric-looking cloud decks you can dive into, god rays, rotor blur, downwash stirring the cloud tops, tracer-bright rounds with travel time and drop. HOOK: a steady hover is a steady shot. Flying fast makes you hard to hit but your sight swings with the airframe; alt = HOVER HOLD (auto-hover and zoom: a rock-steady sight, but you hang still in the open). Cloud is the cover: inside it you are hidden and blind, your rotor wash carving a visible hole that gives you away; peaks and towers block shots. Open distance is the whole sky: close in through cloud, or take the long shot across a clear lane and lead it. THE WORLD INTERFERES: an airliner crossing on its flight path, a flock of geese, a hot-air balloon festival drifting through, lightning inside a storm cell that lights up silhouettes, a search-and-rescue heli, wind gusts that shove both aircraft (all from the seed and ctx.time). Abilities, for example: FLARES (a burst of bright decoys that blinds the scope and hides you for a moment: smoke) and RADAR SWEEP (one sweep that marks the rival through cloud for two seconds and tells them they were painted: recon). Only a rifle round from the other sniper scores; nothing else can kill. Kill moment: the hit helicopter's rotor stutters, it autorotates down in a slow spiral trailing coloured smoke and its pilot bails out under a parachute in the rival's colour, bloodless and almost graceful, as the winner's helicopter circles once.

dims.name: LEVIATHAN RUN
dims.brief: PERSPECTIVE: side-on, rendered in real 3D (a 2.5D profile view with deep parallax: the only side-on world in the game that is 3D, so depth, scale and atmosphere are the point). SETTING: a desert planet under two suns and a ringed gas giant, endless dunes, rock spires, wind-blown sand. Each sniper rides the back of their own colossal sand leviathan: a segmented, armoured burrowing creature hundreds of metres long that swims through the dunes like a whale through swell, throwing up walls of sand. Inspired by the grandeur of desert-planet science fiction, but an ORIGINAL design: invent the creature, the riders, their gear and every name; nothing may copy an existing book, film or game. renderer 'three', aim 'pointer' or 'look' as plays best. The two leviathans run side by side or one behind the other across the frame, sometimes hundreds of metres apart and sometimes surging close; the camera frames both riders and pulls back to show the full scale. You run and jump along your leviathan's back like a platformer (its plates and dorsal spines are the cover, and its body arches and flexes under you), and can LEAP across when the two beasts swing together to fight at close quarters on the same back. HOOK: the ground you stand on is alive. Each leviathan rises, arches and dives on a rhythm timed from the seed and ctx.time: when its back goes under you must be on a segment that stays above the sand or grab a spine and ride it out (aim wrecked while you hang on); a breach lifts you high for a clear long shot. Rounds are slow, heavy, visible bolts with drop, deflected by the wind in a sandstorm; alt = PLANT (hook into a plate: rock-steady aim, cannot move, exposed). THE WORLD INTERFERES: a sandstorm front that cuts visibility to silhouettes, lightning in the dust, a third wild leviathan breaching between the two, flocks of leathery fliers, a caravan of walkers on a far ridge, falling rock from a spire the beasts brush past. Abilities, for example: THUMPER (a planted pulse that makes your beast surge or dive on command) and DUST CLOAK (kick up a wall of sand along the back: smoke). Only a bolt from the other sniper scores; a fall into the sand shoves you back onto the beast shaken, never kills. Kill moment: the hit rider is knocked off in slow motion and tumbles down the flank in a river of sand as their leviathan sounds a huge mournful call and dives, the winner's beast breaching against the suns.

fx.name: DO YOU WANT TO DEVELOP AN APP?
fx.brief: THIS IS THE REVEAL. The mode is called 'Do you want to develop an app?' and until this moment the players believe they are in the ordinary long-range valley duel: this transition is reserved for the FIRST point of every match, is never seen again in that match, and is the moment the game shows its hand. A first-time player should be left stunned and laughing. CONCEPT: the game is hijacked by its own making. The old world freezes on the end of the round; a beat of silence; then a perfectly ordinary, slightly-too-cheerful system dialog (your own clean, rounded, modern design — not a copy of any real operating system) pops up dead centre with a soft chime and asks: 'Do you want to develop an app?' — two buttons. A mouse cursor drifts in on its own, heads for [No]... and the gag lands (the No button slides away, or relabels itself 'Yes', or both buttons say Yes, or a 'Remind me later' turns out to be Yes too, or a countdown auto-accepts — chosen by seed). Click. TAKEOVER: the old world shrinks into the preview pane of an IDE / app-builder window that assembles itself around it — file tree, tabs, console — and code TYPES ITSELF at speed, genuinely describing the next world from the context: new Dimension("<to name>"), perspective: "<to perspective>", palette swatches in the new world's real colours, players: ["<winner>", "<loser>"], comments that mock the kill by name ('// <loser> did not see that coming', '// TODO: teach <loser> about cover'), the score as a constant. The preview pane flickers through wireframes and placeholder boxes; a build bar runs with comically specific steps ('Compiling shaders…', 'Linking snipers…', 'Bundling physics…', 'Removing the valley…') and a rare error that fixes itself; BUILD SUCCEEDED; the Run button presses itself; white flash (the swap). ARRIVAL: the app launches — the IDE's panels fly apart and the preview pane expands to fill the screen as the live new world, with a small toast: 'App launched: <to name>'. The comedy is contrast: the first second must be deadpan and quiet after a tense military duel, then it escalates relentlessly. Typography and UI craft must be immaculate (this is a parody of polished software, so it has to BE polished): real layout, syntax colouring, easing on every window move, cursor blink, satisfying key and click sounds. Vary by seed: the dialog gag, the IDE theme (dark, light, retro beige), the code and comments, the build steps, the toast.

fx.name: LAST SYNAPSE
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the last thing the loser's brain ever does in this world. The old world is pulled into the loser's eye / through the scope glass and we plunge to the microscopic scale: a dark forest of glowing NEURONS — branching dendrites, pulsing somas, drifting neurotransmitter motes with depth of field. An action potential ignites at one neuron and races along a myelinated axon (saltatory jumps of light from node to node), the camera chasing it through the branching network, picking up speed, other pathways lighting in the colours of the two snipers. It reaches the final synaptic terminal: vesicles burst, a storm of sparks crosses the cleft — and the discharge is the white-out that carries both players into the new dimension (the swap), with the new world's palette already flooding the network just before it. Arrival: the neural tree itself re-forms into the outline of the new world, or the lightning afterimage fades off it. Vary by seed: the network's shape, the route and number of hops, the camera path, the colour scheme of the tissue, what faint memory-images flicker inside the cells. All stylized light and electricity.

fx.name: LIFE FLASH
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the loser's life flashes before their eyes. Freeze the old world; push in hard on the impact point until it becomes a stylized close-up of the loser's face / eye (drawn in code: simple, graphic, in their identity colour, a flicker of surprise), then through the pupil into a rapid-fire MEMORY MONTAGE: a timeline of their life as vignettes drawn procedurally in a warm home-movie style — baby's first steps, a birthday cake, learning to ride a bike, a first day of school, a paper target at a funfair, graduation, a first rifle on a range, a wedding, the handshake before this duel — each a small animated scene framed as Super-8 film, a Polaroid, a VHS still or a photo-album page, with dates and handwritten captions that use the loser's name. They come faster and faster, the years counting up on screen, film burning and sprocket holes flying, until the reel runs out and burns white (the swap). Arrival: a new memory develops like a Polaroid, in the new world's palette — it is the new dimension, and its name is the caption. Vary by seed: which six or seven memories (from a pool of at least fourteen), their order within the life, the film stock / framing device, the captions, the home town, the year of birth. If the round was a draw, both snipers share the reel.

fx.name: BROKEN REALITY
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the kill shot cracks the world like a pane of glass. Cracks race out from the impact point (ctx.focus) across the frozen old world with a sharp ping; a beat of silence; then reality SHATTERS — the old image breaks into dozens of real 3D shards (a Voronoi-style fracture of a plane textured with fromImage, each shard with thickness, bevelled edges catching light, refracting what is behind it) that tumble toward the camera and fall away into a void. Behind the glass is the space between dimensions: a deep volume lit in the new world's palette with drifting fragments of other realities. The camera pushes through the falling glass; at the swap a second, intact pane rushes up out of the dark, catches the light (white glint = the swap), and it is the new world — whose own shards then fly in reverse and seal themselves, the last crack healing with a shimmer. Vary by seed: the fracture pattern and shard count, which way the glass falls (toward camera, sucked away, spun), the void's contents, the camera move, whether the new world assembles from shards or wipes in through a healing crack.

fx.name: EVENT HORIZON
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the bullet punches a hole in spacetime. A point of absolute black opens at the impact point and becomes a BLACK HOLE: gravitational lensing bends the old world around it (the image stretches into arcs and an Einstein ring), the picture spaghettifies and is drawn into a glowing accretion disk in the old world's colours, and the camera falls in. Then the ride: a relativistic tunnel — starlight blue-shifting into streaks, rings of warped light rushing past, the tunnel walls made of smeared fragments of the old world giving way to the new world's palette, the two snipers' colours spiralling around each other like twin photon trails, the hum rising. At the far mouth: a white ring that swallows the frame (the swap), and we are spat out — the new world unwraps from a sphere / de-lenses from an Einstein ring back into a flat picture. Vary by seed: the hole's spin direction and disk tilt, the tunnel's geometry (round, hexagonal, braided, a helix), its curve and roll, what debris rides along, the palette progression.

fx.name: CHANNEL SURF
fx.brief: CONCEPT: somebody changes the channel on reality. The old world turns out to be on a television: it bulges into CRT curvature, scanlines and phosphor glow fade up, the camera pulls back to a chunky old TV set in a dark living room (lit only by the screen, drawn in code), a channel number in the corner. Then a click — the picture collapses to a line and a dot the way old sets switch off, static, and the unseen viewer starts SURFING: a rapid run of four to six procedurally drawn fake channels, each a tiny, funny, fully animated vignette with its own on-screen graphics — a weather map with a storm shaped like a crosshair, a cooking show, a shopping channel selling the winner's rifle, a nature documentary, a late-night test card, a news ticker reporting THIS kill by name ('BREAKING: <winner> lands <how> on <loser>'), a sports score showing the real match score — with tracking glitches, colour bleed and the kachunk of a dial between them. A burst of white static (the swap), and the dial lands on the new dimension's channel with an OSD caption of its name; the camera pushes into the glass until the scanlines and curvature fall away and the live world is all there is. Vary by seed: which channels, their order and content details, the TV's model and room, the channel numbers, the surfing rhythm.

fx.name: POWERS OF TEN
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the camera pulls back from the duel and does not stop. The old world shrinks to a tiny glowing rectangle on the face of a planet; the planet falls away to a dot in its solar system (orbits drawn as fine lines), the star becomes one of billions in a spiral galaxy, the galaxy one of a foam of clusters, the cosmic web itself curls into — a twist chosen by seed — a marble in a child's hand, a glint in the winner's scope lens, a single neuron, a drop on a petri dish, a pixel on a screen. A clean technical readout ticks up the scale the whole way (10^3 m, 10^9 m, 10^21 m ...) with the names of what we are passing. A held beat at the top, a flash (the swap), and the dive back in — but somewhere else: down through a different galaxy, a different star, a planet in the new world's colours, through cloud, to a rectangle that grows until it is the new dimension. Each scale level is its own beautiful procedural picture with parallax, and the zoom is one continuous, accelerating then decelerating move. Vary by seed: the twist at the top, the look of the planets / galaxy, the route back down, the labels.

fx.name: THROUGH AND THROUGH
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the bullet does not stop — follow it. Bullet time: the old world freezes at the moment of impact, colour draining except for the winner's colour; the camera swings around to ride just behind the round as it leaves the frame's surface — because the world is a surface: the bullet PUNCHES THROUGH the picture, leaving a torn hole with curled paper / shattered-screen edges at the impact point, and we dive through after it. Inside: the space between dimensions as a rifled barrel of light — spiralling grooves, shock diamonds off the bullet's nose, sparks, the walls flickering with slices of the old world that peel away as slices of the new world's palette take over; the bullet itself is a beautiful object, glowing in the winner's colour, engraved with the loser's name. Ahead, a disc of light grows: the back of the next world. The bullet strikes it (the swap is the white impact), and from the other side we see the new world's picture bulge, tear and burst outward in a ring of fragments as the round exits — the hole seals behind us, the fragments settle into the new world, a last ripple, a spent casing tumbling past the lens. Vary by seed: the entry tear style, the tunnel's twist rate and colour story, obstacles the bullet passes through (panes, playing cards, apples, older worlds), the camera roll, the exit style.

fx.name: TURN THE PAGE
fx.brief: CONCEPT: it was all a story, and the page turns. The old world flattens into a printed illustration on the page of a huge old STORYBOOK lying open on a desk by candlelight (3D: a camera pulling back from a page mesh textured with fromImage, paper grain, a deckled edge, the facing page set in serif type). A narrator's line writes itself beneath the picture in ink — about this kill, by name: 'And so <loser> fell to a single shot, and <winner> thought the tale was done.' A hand-drawn flourish; then the page lifts and TURNS with a proper curl (a vertex-shader page bend with a shadow underneath and the back of the paper showing through), and another, and another — a flurry of leaves riffling past, each glimpsed spread a different illustrated world, the candle guttering — until the book lands on a new spread (a blank bright page is the swap) where the new dimension's picture inks itself in / pops up as a paper pop-up, with a chapter heading in drop-cap lettering: 'Chapter <round>: <to name>'. The camera pushes in until the page is the world. Vary by seed: the narration (several templates), the book's binding and desk dressing, the number and content of riffled pages, the direction of the turn, the typography, whether the arrival inks in, unfolds as a pop-up or is revealed by a pressed flower sliding away.

fx.name: COSMIC SLOTS
fx.brief: CONCEPT: fate pulls the lever. The old world shrinks back onto a small screen set in the top of a colossal chrome-and-neon SLOT MACHINE floating in a starry void (drawn in code with real showmanship: chasing marquee bulbs, brushed metal, glass reflections, a jackpot sign reading MULTIVERSE). The winner's name lights up on the marquee; the lever cranks down by itself with a mechanical clunk; three reels labelled PERSPECTIVE, WORLD and RULES blur into motion, their symbols and words flying past (real candidates mixed with absurd fakes: 'UPSIDE DOWN', 'ALL SOUP', 'BEES'). They stop one at a time with weighty ka-chunks — a near-miss tease on the second — landing on the truth: the new dimension's perspective, its name, and a tagline. JACKPOT: bells, strobing bulbs, a fountain of coins in the winner's colour pouring toward the camera until they fill the frame white-gold (the swap), and the coins part / the reel window irises open onto the new world. Vary by seed: the machine's styling and colourway, the fake reel entries, the tease, the order the reels stop, the payout (coins, tokens, tiny rifles, stars), the camera move.

fx.name: CONTINUE?
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the arcade game-over screen. The old world freezes, drains to greyscale and crunches down into fat pixels; huge chrome arcade lettering drops in — GAME OVER for the loser, by name — and then the classic taunt: 'CONTINUE? 9 … 8 … 7 …' with a coin slot glowing below, the count thumping down with a heartbeat, the loser's name blinking. Around it, proper arcade dressing drawn in code: a high-score table that shows the real match score with both snipers' names, a bonus tally for the round just played that rattles up in the winner's colour ('DISTANCE', 'STYLE: <how>', 'MERCY: 0'), scanlines and bloom. At the last moment a coin spins through the air in slow motion (a little gag on the way, chosen by seed: it hits the rim, a hand fumbles it, the count freezes at 1 to wait for it) and drops into the slot — CREDIT 1 — 'PLAYER <loser> CONTINUES'. Then a stage card in the new world's palette, attract-mode style: 'STAGE <round + 1>' and the new dimension's name and perspective sweeping in over a moving starfield or checkerboard, 'READY?' flashing — the flash is the swap — and the new world arrives through an arcade wipe (pixel dissolve, venetian blinds, expanding diamonds: by seed). Vary by seed: the cabinet's era and art style (80s vector, 90s chrome, 2000s gloss), the coin gag, the tally lines, the wipe, the announcer text. If the round was a draw: 'DRAW GAME — BOTH PLAYERS CONTINUE' and two coins.

fx.name: RESPAWN OF THE SPECIES
fx.brief: CONCEPT: the loser has to start again — from the very beginning. The old world dissolves into bubbles and sinks into a warm PRIMORDIAL SOUP. From the soup, a fast-forward of all of evolution as one continuous morphing silhouette drawn with museum-diagram charm: a wriggling cell, a fish, a thing that crawls onto a beach, a small dinosaur (a meteor streaks by behind), a shrew, an ape that picks up a stick — and here the joke lands — the stick becomes a longer stick, a spear, a musket, a scoped rifle, as the figure straightens through the famous march-of-progress line-up into a modern sniper in the loser's colour, with a geological time ruler racing along the bottom of the frame ('3.8 BILLION YEARS AGO' ... 'LAST TUESDAY' ... 'NOW'). The winner's silhouette is already there waiting at the end of the line, checking a watch. The two raise their rifles, a muzzle flash whites out the frame (the swap), and the backdrop behind the figures is the new world, already in progress. Vary by seed: which creatures appear in the line-up (pool of at least twelve), the background eras and their gags, the labels on the ruler, the final pose, the colour treatment (museum chart, cave painting, textbook plate).

fx.name: GOING UP
fx.brief: CONCEPT: deadpan comedy as contrast — reality has an elevator. Polished brass ELEVATOR DOORS slide shut over the old world with a soft thunk, and both snipers are suddenly just two silhouettes standing awkwardly side by side in a lift (seen from behind, in their colours, rifles held like umbrellas; the winner taps a foot, the loser steams slightly), while gentle bossa-nova muzak plays (a real little tune on ctx.audio.music) and a floor indicator above the doors ticks through dimensions: an arrow sweeping a brass dial or a flip-dot display reading floor names — real ones and absurd fakes ('B2: REGRETS', '14: BEES', '41: ALL SOUP') — passing the old world's name and heading for the new one's. Small gags sell the wait: a flickering light, a notice on the wall with the current score, one sniper pressing the button again. DING. The indicator lands on the new dimension's name; the doors part with a blaze of light from outside in the new world's palette (the swap is the white of the opening doors) and the camera rides out between them into the world. Vary by seed: the lift's decor (art deco, wood panel, brutalist, space station), the floors passed, which gags play, the muzak's key and tempo, how far the lift travels.

fx.name: PLUNGE
fx.brief: A LINKING transition, used in exactly one place: from the surfing world (third person, golden-hour ocean; its last frame is the camera crossing the waterline as the winner dives in after the surfer they just shot off a board) to the underwater world THE DEEP (first person spearfishing over a reef wall; its first frame is just below the surface looking down). It must feel like ONE continuous dive, not an effect laid over two pictures: the from-image is swallowed by a churning curtain of foam and bubbles as the lens goes under; sound drops from surf roar to a muffled underwater hush with a single deep breath; the golden light turns to blue-green; through the clearing bubbles two silhouettes fall — the one who was shot, tumbling, and the one who dived, arrow-straight — and as they sink their beach gear trades itself for diving gear in passing (a board leash becomes a fin strap, sunglasses become a mask, the rifle becomes a speargun) in a few light, readable beats; sunlight shafts sweep through, a school of fish parts around the camera, something enormous moves far below for a single frame; then the last bubbles rise away to leave the to-image. Swap under the thickest bubbles. Around 4 to 5 seconds. It should be beautiful and calm after the chaos of the wipe-out: the breath before the next duel. Test it with --from surf --to abyss as soon as both worlds exist; until then use the examples.

fx.name: TOWER CONTROL
fx.brief: The from-image shrinks to a blip: the camera pulls back and it becomes a glowing return on a circular radar scope, and we are inside a dim air traffic control tower at night — the green sweep arm turning, range rings, flight strips, the glow of consoles on glass, rain on the windows and runway lights beyond. The sweep passes and PINGS the blip (a clean sonar-like tone); with each pass the scope picks up more: two contacts closing on each other, callsigns in the two players' colours, a conflict alert flashing. A controller's hand slides a flight strip across the board that reads the name of the next world as a destination; a voice-like synthesized radio squelch; the sweep comes round one last time and on that ping the scope zooms into the new contact, which resolves into the to-image. Swap under the brightest ping bloom. Around 9 to 11 seconds, original design throughout (no real airline, airport or agency names or logos).

fx.name: FIRST LIGHT
fx.brief: The from-image dims and becomes a picture on an astronomer's monitor in a mountaintop observatory at night; the camera pulls back through the control room and out into a colossal dome as its shutter splits open to a field of stars. Inside sits an impossibly large, super-powered space telescope: a segmented golden mirror many storeys across, a truss the size of a stadium, cables and frost. It slews with deep machinery groans, the dome rotates, warning lamps turn, and the mirror segments ripple into alignment one by one. Then FIRST LIGHT: the camera dives down the tube, bounces off the mirror and rides the telescope's gaze outward: the atmosphere's shimmer falls away, the moon, planets and their rings sweep past, the focus racks in stages (each stage a soft mechanical clunk and a sharpening of the image) through nebulae and star fields to a single faint point that resolves, with diffraction spikes, into a tiny world: the to-image, seen first as a grainy false-colour exposure that snaps into full clarity. Swap under the brightest diffraction flare. Around 10 to 12 seconds. Awe and quiet rather than chaos; an original observatory and instrument (no real telescope's name, logo or exact design).

fx.name: KERNEL PANIC
fx.brief: THE EXIT FROM THE TERMINAL WORLD (id 'terminal', TTY DUEL: a top-down duel drawn entirely in text characters on a CRT). The kill crashes the program. The from-image freezes mid-frame, characters start to corrupt and smear down the screen, and the terminal throws a fault in its own typeface: a 'segmentation fault' line naming the loser, then a full kernel panic that scrolls a stack trace whose function names tell the story of the kill (the winner's name, the kill label, the range), a hex dump whose ASCII column spells a taunt, a blinking 'rebooting in 3'. The tube collapses to a line and a dot. A beat of black and a relay click. Then an original firmware power-on self test: memory counting up, devices detected ('2 snipers found'), a boot menu listing dimensions as bootable systems with the cursor skipping past a few and choosing the next world by name, a loader bar drawn in block characters. The bar's blocks then turn out to be the first row of the to-image arriving as coarse character cells that refine, cell by cell, into the real picture (swap under the densest text). This is a WORLD'S OWN EXIT: it is only ever played when a kill ends a round in that one world, so build it around what that world is and make the hand-over from its last frame feel inevitable, as if the world itself were doing it. Read that world's code and look at its screenshots first (do not edit it) and borrow its palette, lettering and sound character. It must still leave to ANY next world (the to-image can be anything), and should make the arrival feel like part of the same joke. Clever and specific beats big: 6 to 9 seconds. Original designs throughout: no real console, computer, operating system, publisher or studio names, logos or boot screens.

fx.name: BLOW ON IT
fx.brief: THE EXIT FROM THE PIXEL-ART WORLD (id 'pixel', CARTRIDGE CANYON: a side-on retro pixel platformer duel). The kill makes the game glitch the way a dirty cartridge does: the from-image tears into garbage tiles, sprites duplicate in columns, the palette swaps, a stuck square-wave note drones, and the picture locks up. The camera pulls back and the frozen frame is on a small bulging CRT television on a bedroom carpet at night, wired to an original chunky home console with a top-loading cartridge slot. A hand reaches in, thumps the console once (the picture jumps and gets worse), flicks the power off, yanks the cartridge out, blows across its contacts (a puff of dust in the TV glow), considers it, tosses it on a pile of others, and picks a different cartridge whose hand-written label is the next world's name in the next world's colours. Slot, press, power: a snowy screen, an original two-note boot jingle, and the to-image rolls into vertical hold on the tube. The camera pushes back into the glass until the scanlines and curvature fall away and it is simply the new world (swap while the tube is dark between cartridges). This is a WORLD'S OWN EXIT: it is only ever played when a kill ends a round in that one world, so build it around what that world is and make the hand-over from its last frame feel inevitable, as if the world itself were doing it. Read that world's code and look at its screenshots first (do not edit it) and borrow its palette, lettering and sound character. It must still leave to ANY next world (the to-image can be anything), and should make the arrival feel like part of the same joke. Clever and specific beats big: 6 to 9 seconds. Original designs throughout: no real console, computer, operating system, publisher or studio names, logos or boot screens.

fx.name: TIDY-UP TIME
fx.brief: THE EXIT FROM THE TOY WORLD (id 'toybox', TOY BOX: plastic riflemen duelling on a bedroom rug among blocks, books, dominoes and a wooden train, top-down 3D). The kill is followed by a grown-up's muffled voice-like call from beyond the door (a synthesized, wordless 'tidy-up time' cadence) and the big ceiling light snapping on, flattening the moody lamp light. The camera rises to a child's-eye height and enormous hands sweep in: they scoop the fallen soldier, stand the winner on a shelf like a trophy, sweep blocks and dominoes with a forearm, lift the train, and drop everything into an open wooden toy box whose inside we fall into with the toys. The lid comes down: darkness, the rattle of toys settling, a thin line of light at the lid's edge, a music-box phrase winding down. Then the lid lifts again, and what the hands take out and set on the floor is a new toy that IS the next world: the to-image seen first as the printed lid of a game box, a pop-up book spread or a snow-globe (pick by seed), which the camera dives into until it fills the frame (swap in the dark of the closed box). Warm, funny, slightly huge and uncanny from a toy's point of view; hands only, never a face. This is a WORLD'S OWN EXIT: it is only ever played when a kill ends a round in that one world, so build it around what that world is and make the hand-over from its last frame feel inevitable, as if the world itself were doing it. Read that world's code and look at its screenshots first (do not edit it) and borrow its palette, lettering and sound character. It must still leave to ANY next world (the to-image can be anything), and should make the arrival feel like part of the same joke. Clever and specific beats big: 6 to 9 seconds. Original designs throughout: no real console, computer, operating system, publisher or studio names, logos or boot screens.

fx.name: TO BE CONTINUED
fx.brief: THE EXIT FROM THE MANGA WORLD (id 'manga', INK DUEL: a side-on duel inked in black and white like a manga page). The from-image stops being a moving picture and becomes the last panel of a printed page: it gains a panel border and screentone, the camera pulls back and the rest of the page draws itself in around it in fast confident brush strokes, three or four panels that retell the kill (a close-up of the winner's eye, the shot as speed lines, the loser's silhouette, a sound-effect lettered across the gutter) with the winner's and loser's names in caption boxes. The page is in a thick anthology magazine held in two hands. A 'to be continued' box lands in the corner with a stamp sound. A thumb lifts the corner and the page turns the way manga reads, right to left, with real paper curl, show-through of the ink on the back and the fan of pages beneath; for a few frames we see other pages flick past (glimpses of other worlds as inked thumbnails). It stops on a full-page splash: a chapter title page whose title is the next world's name, drawn in ink, which then floods with the next world's colour from the centre out as the to-image takes over the page and the paper edges slide out of frame (swap as the turning page fills the frame). This is a WORLD'S OWN EXIT: it is only ever played when a kill ends a round in that one world, so build it around what that world is and make the hand-over from its last frame feel inevitable, as if the world itself were doing it. fx.name: SWALLOWED
fx.brief: THE EXIT FROM THE UNDERWATER WORLD (id 'abyss', THE DEEP: first-person spearfishing over a reef wall, with a giant kraken below). The kraken, which never kills during the duel, finally takes an interest. As the from-image holds, the light dims and a vast shape rises behind the drifting loser: arms unfurl around the frame from every edge, suckers and blue photophores sliding past the lens, and the great amber eye fills the screen and looks straight at the player. It blinks. A jet of ink swallows everything to black, with a sub-bass groan. In the dark, bioluminescent specks drift and gather; they swirl into a slow spiral, a galaxy of them, and begin to outline shapes, which are the silhouettes of the next world drawn in points of light.
